title: Conservative Contextual Bandits: Beyond Linear Representations

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable conservative contextual bandits for general non-linear cost functions, which prior UCB-based methods (limited to multi-armed and linear settings) could not handle. Papers [1], [2], [5], [6], [7], [11], [12], and [19] all address safety-constrained or conservative contextual bandits, but they are limited to linear or multi-armed settings. None of these papers explicitly extend to general non-linear cost functions. Therefore, the specific purpose of handling general non-linear cost functions under safety constraints is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves reducing the conservative bandit problem to a black-box online regression oracle with squared loss, using Inverse Gap Weighting (IGW) exploration and switching to the baseline action when a safety condition is violated. Papers [9], [10], and [13] discuss reductions from contextual bandits to online regression oracles, including squared loss. However, none of these papers incorporate the specific IGW exploration strategy or the novel analysis bounding \( n_T \) (times the baseline is played) by relating it to squared regression loss instead of UCB confidence sets. Thus, the mechanism is **not covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation proves regret bounds \( O(\sqrt{K T \text{Reg}_\text{Sq}(T)} + K \text{Reg}_\text{Sq}(T)/\alpha) \) with the \((1+\alpha)\) performance constraint satisfied with high probability. Papers [9], [10], and [13] use similar evaluation designs involving regret bounds derived from reductions to regression oracles. While the specific regret bound and performance constraint differ in detail, the evaluation design (proving regret bounds via reductions to regression oracles) is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is safe/conservative contextual bandits. Papers [1], [2], [5], [6], [7], [11], [12], and [19] all operate in the same general application area of safe or conservative contextual bandits. While this contribution targets a specific extension to non-linear cost functions, the domain itself is **covered**.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to obtain a sharper, data-dependent (first-order) regret guarantee for conservative bandits that scales with the optimal policy's cumulative loss \( L^* \) rather than the horizon \( T \). Paper [5] explicitly discusses first-order regret bounds for contextual bandits, stating that "the more refined concept of first-order regret bound replaces this with a scaling \(\sqrt{L^*}\), which may be much smaller than \(\sqrt{T}\)." This matches the objective of improving regret guarantees to scale with \( L^* \). Additionally, paper [21] identifies first-order regret bounds for contextual bandits as an open problem, which aligns with the contribution's purpose of addressing this gap. Therefore, the purpose is covered.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves reducing to an online regression oracle with KL loss and using an episodic, time-dependent exploration parameter \(\gamma_t\) (constant within each of \(\log(L^*)\) episodes) to avoid a \(\sqrt{T}\) dependence. Paper [18] provides a universal reduction from contextual bandits to online regression, stating, "We provide the first universal and optimal reduction from contextual bandits to online regression." This reduction matches the mechanism's core primitive of leveraging regression oracles. Paper [8] also discusses contextual bandits with feedback graphs based on reduction to regression, which is conceptually equivalent. However, neither paper explicitly uses KL loss or episodic exploration parameters like \(\gamma_t\), so the specific mechanism is not fully covered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation proves first-order regret bounds \( O(\sqrt{K L^* \log(L^*) \text{Reg}_{KL}(T)} + K \text{Reg}_{KL}(T)(1+1/\alpha)) \) with performance constraints satisfied with high probability (Theorem 4.1). Paper [5] discusses first-order regret bounds for contextual bandits, stating, "Regret bounds in online learning compare the player's performance to \( L^* \), the optimal performance in hindsight with a fixed strategy." Paper [18] also proves regret bounds for contextual bandits reduced to regression oracles. Both papers use similar evaluation designs (proving regret bounds with respect to \( L^* \)), so the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is safe/conservative contextual bandits. Papers [1], [2], [4], [10], [13], [14], [17], [19], and [22] all address conservative or safe contextual bandits, with safety constraints or performance guarantees as a central theme. For example, paper [13] studies "a family of conservative bandit problems (CBPs) with sample-path reward constraints," and paper [14] introduces "safe linear stochastic bandits" with safety thresholds. These papers collectively cover the domain of safe/conservative contextual bandits.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to provide concrete end-to-end guarantees by instantiating the abstract oracle with a neural network and validating empirically. Paper [11] ("Contextual Bandits with Online Neural Regression") shares the same purpose at the problem-class level, as it investigates neural networks for online regression and contextual bandits, leveraging realizability assumptions to provide regret guarantees. The objective of both papers is to close the gap between theoretical guarantees and practical implementation in neural contextual bandits.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves instantiating the online regression oracle with Online Gradient Descent (OGD) over a feed-forward neural network, leveraging O(log T) neural-regression regret. Paper [4] ("Proximal Online Gradient Is Optimum for Dynamic Regret") establishes OGD as optimal for dynamic regret in online learning, and Paper [11] ("Contextual Bandits with Online Neural Regression") applies neural networks to online regression in contextual bandits, achieving sublinear regret bounds. Both papers use substantively equivalent primitives: OGD for online regression and neural networks for contextual bandits.

The evaluation design includes theoretical regret bounds (~O(sqrt(KT)+K/alpha) and ~O(sqrt(K L*)+K(1+1/alpha)) in Thms 5.1 and 5.2) and empirical validation on openml multiclass-classification bandit datasets, comparing sublinear regret and constraint-violation percentages against baselines. Paper [11] ("Contextual Bandits with Online Neural Regression") uses the same evaluation design: theoretical regret bounds for neural contextual bandits and empirical validation on contextual bandit datasets. The benchmark family (contextual bandit datasets) and metric semantics (regret bounds and constraint violations) are substantively equivalent.

### Domain
The domain is neural contextual bandits with empirical validation. Paper [6] ("Provably and Practically Efficient Neural Contextual Bandits") and Paper [11] ("Contextual Bandits with Online Neural Regression") both operate in the same general application area of neural contextual bandits, addressing similar problems of regret minimization and empirical validation.
